title: Observability: Cost vs Latency Tradeoffs — Guide for Product and Platform Teams
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This guide explains how product managers and platform engineers should interpret and act on observability signals when balancing cost and latency for Redwood-hosted and dedicated inference routes. It provides concrete configuration patterns, decision criteria, and rollout steps so teams can make consistent trade-offs that align with SLOs and customer commitments.

Audience:
- Product managers owning per-route SLAs and fidelity budgets
- Platform engineers who tune runtime parameters (batching, caching, quantization, prefetch)
- Reliability engineers monitoring and responding to sustained regressions in cost or latency

Executive summary:
- Observability signals (token-level cost, p50/p95 latency, queue depth, batch size distribution, cache hit ratio) should drive automated and manual levers in a prioritized order: routing policy, batch sizing, cache sizing, quantization profile, then model variant fallback.
- Use a 3‑tier decision matrix (Latency-critical, Balanced, Cost‑sensitive) to choose defaults and escalation policies.
- Instrument per-route observability dashboards to expose 5 core metrics and one derived cost-efficiency score.

Key definitions and target SLO mappings:
- Latency SLO: request p95 < target_ms (per-route). Typical tiers: Critical (p95 < 200ms), Standard (p95 < 400ms), Flexible (p95 < 800ms).
- Cost SLO: tokens / $ metric (tokens-per-dollar) or cost-per-request budget. Teams should set a monthly cost-per-route budget and a 7‑day running cost drift alert.
- Fidelity bucket: Low / Medium / High model variants or quantization levels that impact quality.

Five primary observability signals (what to watch) and how to interpret them:
1) Token-level cost (usd/token broken down by model and variant) — sudden increase typically indicates a model switch or rollout misconfiguration.
2) p95 generation latency (ms) — primary indicator for user-facing latency regressions.
3) Batch size distribution (mean, median, tail) — high variance suggests misaligned batching policy for the workload.
4) KV/prefix cache hit ratio — low values indicate ineffective caching or poor prefix reuse; directly increases per-token cost.
5) Queue length / request concurrency — sustained queues at the worker layer point to capacity limits or throttling.

Decision framework (three tiers)
- Latency-critical routes
  - Default: aggressive prefetch, single-request batching (batch size cap 1–4), higher provisioned capacity (dedicated or reserved), High fidelity model variant.
  - Observability thresholds: p95 > target_ms for 5 minutes -> immediate scale-up (automated), p95 > target_ms for 15 minutes -> temporary downgrade of fidelity only if customer permits fallback.
  - Cost tradeoff: Accepts ~2–5x token cost increase vs Balanced.

- Balanced routes
  - Default: adaptive batching (target mean batch 8–24 tokens), 1–2s KV cache retention, Medium fidelity variant.
  - Observability thresholds: p95 drift +10% for 15 minutes -> suggest policy change (batch window reduction) and run predictive-scaling simulation.

- Cost-sensitive routes
  - Default: larger batching windows (batch mean 32–128 tokens), long prefix caching (10–30s or more), quantized model variants as default.
  - Observability thresholds: tokens-per-$ drops >15% for 24 hours -> automatically recommend quantization or route migration to low-cost tier.

Recommended observability dashboards (minimum widgets)
- Route overview: p50/p95 latency sparkline, tokens-per-$, 24h cost, error rate
- Kernel/worker health: queue depth, worker CPU/GPU utilization, memory pressure
- Batching characteristics: batch size histogram, mean batch latency, inter-arrival time distribution
- Cache effectiveness: hit ratio, average cached prefix length, bytes saved per hour
- Rollout monitor: model variant distribution, per-variant latency and cost

Decision matrix (quick reference)
| Metric | Action (Immediate, 0–5m) | Action (Short, 5–60m) | Owner | Tooling/Playbook |
|--------|--------------------------|-----------------------|-------|------------------|
| p95 latency spike | Scale/route away traffic to standby region (automated) | If persists, reduce batch window and enable lower-fidelity fallback | SRE/Platform | Autoscaler + routing policy |
| Token cost spike | Evaluate per-variant cost, rollback to previous variant | Run local sampling and offline eval vs baseline | Product | Cost lookup + variant rollback |
| Cache hit drop | Clear/rebuild cache, extend prefix retention window | Inspect prefix distribution, increase prefetch for common prefixes | Platform | Cache metrics + prefetch config |
| Batch variance high | Lower batch timeout, increase max outstanding workers | Consider predictive batching config | Runtime team | Batching config APIs |
| Persistent queueing | Add capacity or tune concurrency limits | Temporarily shift non-critical traffic to low-cost tier | SRE | Capacity planner + route migrations |

Configuration examples (YAML snippets teams can apply)
- Adaptive batching (balanced):
  runtime_batching:
    mode: adaptive
    target_mean_batch_size: 16
    max_batch_delay_ms: 50
    allow_cross_tenant: false

- Cache policy (cost-sensitive):
  prefix_cache:
    enabled: true
    retention_seconds: 30
    max_entries: 200000
    eviction: lru

- Quantization/variant policy (automated fallback):
  variant_fallback:
    primary: model-v2-medium
    fallback_order: [model-v2-quantized, model-v1-small]
    fallback_triggers:
      - type: latency
        window: 15m
        threshold_p95_percent: 120
      - type: cost
        window: 24h
        threshold_tokens_per_dollar_drop: 20

Operational runbook (step-by-step)
1) Detect: Alert triggers (p95 or cost drift) — on-call SRE receives alert with route context.
2) Triage (0–10m): Confirm metric integrity (query raw metrics), check recent deploys/rollouts, inspect per-variant distribution.
3) Immediate mitigation (10–30m): Route to standby or increase provisioned capacity. If cost spike, temporarily pause non-critical background routes.
4) Stabilize (30–120m): Apply batching or cache policy adjustments; if quality impacted, coordinate with Product for fallback approval.
5) Post-incident (24–72h): Run cost/quality regressions against saved prompts, author RCA, and apply a permanent config change as appropriate.

Rollout guidance for automated fallbacks and experiments
- Canary first: release variant changes to 1–5% traffic and monitor the rollout panel for both latency and tokens-per-dollars.
- Experiment window: set a mandatory 48–72 hour observation window for cost-latency experiments before expanding traffic.
- Guardrails: never allow automated fallback to reduce fidelity if the customer has explicitly pinned a fidelity variant; instead, notify the customer and offer guidance.

Sample evaluation checklist for product feature owners (pre-release)
- Do we have per-route p95 targets defined? (yes/no)
- Is there a cost budget and 7‑day drift alert? (yes/no)
- Are default runtime policies (batching, caching, quantization) documented for the route? (yes/no)
- Is there a canary rollout defined and an automated rollback threshold? (yes/no)

Appendix A — Common alert thresholds (examples)
- p95 latency increase: +25% sustained for 5 minutes -> page SRE
- tokens-per-$ reduction: -20% sustained for 24 hours -> notify Product and trigger cost-audit playbook
- cache hit ratio drop: <30% sustained for 30 minutes -> suggest prefetched prefixes and longer retention

Appendix B — Example queries
- Tokens-per-dollar (last 24h):
  SELECT sum(tokens) / sum(cost_usd) as tokens_per_dollar FROM metrics WHERE route = 'chat-v1' and ts > now() - interval '24 hours';
- Batch size histogram (last hour):
  SELECT histogram(batch_size) FROM runtime_batches WHERE route = 'summarize' and ts > now() - interval '1 hour';
